entries.meaning: To search, in the mind or in a drawer, for something you need at once.
examples: He cast about for an excuse and found none.
She cast about for the right word for the better part of a minute.
The board has cast about for a replacement since March.
I cast about in the junk drawer for a pen that still worked.
Investors cast about for somewhere safer to park their money.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, which is what fuses the two words into one verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle), normally followed by for
entries.separable: no — nothing can stand between cast and about; what you are hunting for goes after for. ✗ cast an excuse about, ✗ cast it about for.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; the thing sought is introduced by for
entries.register: formal — commoner in writing than in speech; in American speech cast around has largely replaced it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; searching is something you do, and it takes the progressive freely: he was casting about for an excuse.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the prepositional passive fails too: ✗ an excuse was cast about for.
entries.see also: cast around, come up with

entries.meaning: To look around for something or someone, physically or in your memory.
examples: She cast around for a chair that wasn't covered in laundry.
We cast around for a caterer who could take a last-minute job.
He cast around for someone to blame.
After the layoff he cast around for anything that paid.
They have cast around for months without finding a buyer.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on round, never on cast
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle), normally followed by for
entries.separable: no — the phrase stays whole and the object follows for. ✗ cast a plan around, ✗ cast around a plan without for.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; use for to name what you are after
entries.register: everyday — the ordinary American form of cast about
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the everyday American twin of cast about, equally at home in the progressive: she was casting around for a chair.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ a caterer was cast around for.
entries.see also: cast about, come across

entries.meaning: To reject something or someone you no longer have any use for.
examples: She cast aside everything she had been taught about money.
He cast his notes aside and spoke from memory.
Once the season ended, the club cast him aside.
Old loyalties were cast aside in a single afternoon.
Don't cast it aside just because the cover looks dated.
entries.separable: yes — cast aside her doubts and cast her doubts aside are both good, and with a pronoun it must split: cast them aside, never ✗ cast aside them.
entries.register: formal — a written word; in speech Americans say drop, ditch, or throw out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of rejection, not a state.
entries.passive: yes, and common in writing — old loyalties were cast aside in a single afternoon.
entries.see also: cast away, cast off, cast out

entries.meaning: To throw something away; in the passive, to be stranded by a shipwreck.
examples: He cast away the last of his savings on a bad idea.
She cast her fear away and stepped out onto the ice.
You don't get chances like that twice — don't cast it away.
The crew were cast away on a reef two hundred miles from land.
He wrote as if he had been cast away rather than merely transferred to Ohio.

senses.head: Throw away, be rid of
body: Used of things and, more often, of feelings and chances. (отбрасывать, выбрасывать)
examples: He cast away the last of his savings on a bad idea.
She cast her fear away and stepped out onto the ice.
You don't get chances like that twice — don't cast it away.

senses.head: Be shipwrecked
body: Nearly always passive, and the source of the noun castaway. (быть выброшенным на берег после кораблекрушения)
examples: The crew were cast away on a reef two hundred miles from land.
He wrote as if he had been cast away rather than merely transferred to Ohio.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on way; the noun castaway keeps the stress on cast
entries.русский: выбросить, отбросить; (в пассиве) быть выброшенным на необитаемый берег
entries.separable: yes — cast away his fears, cast his fears away, cast them away. The shipwreck sense is almost always passive, so the question rarely arises: they were cast away on an island.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; in sense 2 (shipwreck) the verb survives almost only as a passive participle.
entries.passive: yes — he cast away his savings → his savings were cast away; sense 2 is passive by default: the crew were cast away on a reef.
entries.see also: cast aside, cast off

entries.meaning: To lower the eyes or the head; to leave someone dispirited.
examples: She cast down her eyes when he came into the room.
He cast his gaze down and said nothing.
She raised her eyes for a moment, then cast them down again.
He was cast down by the second rejection in a week.
Nothing cast her down for long.

senses.head: Lower the eyes or the gaze
body: A gesture of modesty or shame. (опускать (глаза, взгляд))
examples: She cast down her eyes when he came into the room.
He cast his gaze down and said nothing.
She raised her eyes for a moment, then cast them down again.

senses.head: Dishearten, dispirit
body: Almost always passive. (повергать в уныние, удручать)
examples: He was cast down by the second rejection in a week.
Nothing cast her down for long.

entries.separable: yes — cast down her eyes, cast her eyes down, cast them down. In the "dishearten" sense the verb survives mainly as the passive participle, where nothing separates: she was cast down by the news.
entries.register: formal — literary and biblical; the modern American equivalents are look down and get someone down
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when you lower your eyes (sense 1); in sense 2 the participle sits close to an adjective of state — she looked cast down.
entries.passive: yes — her eyes were cast down; sense 2 lives in the passive: he was cast down by the second rejection.
entries.see also: cast aside, come down

entries.meaning: To shed something you no longer want; to untie a boat and leave; in knitting, to close off the stitches.
examples: The town has cast off the reputation it had in the eighties.
She cast her coat off and got straight to work.
He cast them off the moment they stopped being useful.
We cast off just after five and were out of the harbor by six.
Knit two more rows, then cast off loosely.

senses.head: Shed, get rid of
body: Used of clothes, habits, rules, and people. (сбрасывать, отвергать)
examples: The town has cast off the reputation it had in the eighties.
She cast her coat off and got straight to work.
He cast them off the moment they stopped being useful.

senses.head: Untie and leave (of a boat)
body: No object; standard among American boaters. (отдавать швартовы, отчаливать)
examples: We cast off just after five and were out of the harbor by six.

senses.head: Finish a knitted piece
body: The last row, where the stitches are closed. (закрывать петли)
examples: Knit two more rows, then cast off loosely.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on off; the noun and adjective castoff move it back to cast
entries.русский: сбросить, отбросить; отдать швартовы; закрыть петли (в вязании)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — cast off the old rules, cast the old rules off, cast them off, never ✗ cast off them. In the boating sense there is no object at all: we cast off at dawn.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you shed something, intransitive when a boat leaves
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: shedding something, leaving a dock, closing off stitches.
entries.passive: restricted — fine where there is an object (the old rules were cast off, the stitches are cast off loosely), impossible in the boating sense, which has none: ✗ was cast off by the crew for we cast off at dawn.
entries.see also: cast on, cast aside, cut loose

entries.meaning: To put the first row of stitches onto a needle, which is how a knitted piece begins.
examples: Cast on forty stitches and join in the round.
She cast eighty stitches on and lost count twice.
Once you have cast them on, knit one row plain.
I cast on last night and I'm already at the cuff.
He cast on too tightly, and the brim won't stretch.
entries.separable: yes — cast on twenty stitches, cast twenty stitches on, cast them on, never ✗ cast on them.
entries.transitive: either — the stitches may be named or simply understood
entries.register: everyday — but only inside knitting; outside the craft it means nothing at all
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a knitting instruction, most often imperative.
entries.passive: restricted — natural as a resulting state (once forty stitches are cast on, join in the round), odd with an agent: ✗ eighty stitches were cast on by her.
entries.see also: cast off

entries.meaning: To drive someone or something out of a place or a community.
examples: The sect cast out anyone who married an outsider.
The village cast the whole family out over a debt nobody could prove.
They cast him out without so much as a hearing.
She was cast out by her own congregation.
The story turns on a healer who casts out what nobody else can see.
Once they decide you don't belong, they cast you out quietly.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on out; the noun outcast reverses the order and the stress
entries.separable: yes — cast out the moneychangers, cast the moneychangers out, cast them out, never ✗ cast out them.
entries.register: formal — biblical in flavor; everyday American is throw out or kick out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of expulsion.
entries.passive: yes, and idiomatic — she was cast out by her own congregation.
entries.see also: cast aside, cast off

entries.meaning: To make a grab at something, usually without getting hold of it, and so to seize on any chance that offers.
examples: She caught at the railing as the bus pulled away.
He caught at my sleeve and asked me to wait.
A drowning man will catch at anything that floats.
They caught at the one figure in the report that helped them.
He catches at every rumor that suits him.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, not a particle — the verb keeps the stress and at reduces to /ət/
entries.separable: no — the object always follows at: catch at a branch, never ✗ catch a branch at. A pronoun stays there too: catch at it.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.register: formal — literary; everyday American is grab at or grab for
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an attempt rather than a result, which is why the generic present works: he catches at every rumor that suits him.
entries.passive: no in practice — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ my sleeve was caught at, ✗ the railing was caught at by her.
entries.see also: catch on, cling to

entries.meaning: To become popular, or to work out what is going on.
examples: The name caught on faster than anyone expected.
Curbside pickup caught on during the pandemic and never went away.
His slang never quite caught on outside the team.
It took me three episodes to catch on.
She caught on to what he was really asking within a minute.
By the time the bank caught on to the scheme, the money was gone.

senses.head: Become popular
body: Of a word, a product, a habit. (прижиться, войти в моду)
examples: The name caught on faster than anyone expected.
Curbside pickup caught on during the pandemic and never went away.
His slang never quite caught on outside the team.

senses.head: Understand, figure it out
body: Often catch on to, and often with a note of "at last." (смекнуть, догадаться, раскусить)
examples: It took me three episodes to catch on.
She caught on to what he was really asking within a minute.
By the time the bank caught on to the scheme, the money was gone.

entries.русский: входить в моду, прижиться; смекнуть, догадаться
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); with to it becomes a three-part verb
entries.separable: no — there is no object to move. When you name what was understood, add to and put it last: catch on to the trick, ✗ catch the trick on.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; catch on to something reaches its object through a preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: sense 1 is a gradual change (the name was catching on), sense 2 a moment of understanding, not a state (it took me three episodes to catch on).
entries.passive: no — intransitive; even with to there is no passive: ✗ the trick was caught on to.
entries.see also: catch up, come around

entries.meaning: To leave someone unprepared, or to expose someone's mistake or lie.
examples: We were caught out by the storm halfway up the trail.
Half the office was caught out when the deadline moved.
Don't let the fine print catch you out.
A single misremembered date caught the witness out.
The follow-up question caught him out.
She caught them out on the dates in their own memo.

senses.head: Be caught unprepared
body: Almost always passive in American use. (быть застигнутым врасплох)
examples: We were caught out by the storm halfway up the trail.
Half the office was caught out when the deadline moved.
Don't let the fine print catch you out.

senses.head: Expose someone's error or lie
body: The active use is chiefly British. (уличить, поймать на ошибке)
examples: A single misremembered date caught the witness out.
The follow-up question caught him out.
She caught them out on the dates in their own memo.

entries.русский: застать врасплох; поймать на ошибке, уличить
entries.separable: yes — catch out the witness, catch the witness out, and with a pronoun it must split: caught her out, never ✗ caught out her.
entries.register: everyday in the passive caught out; chiefly British in the active sense of exposing a lie, where Americans say catch someone in a lie or trip someone up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single event of surprise or exposure.
entries.passive: yes — and sense 1 is essentially passive-only in American use: we were caught out by the storm halfway up the trail.
entries.see also: catch up with, come out

entries.meaning: To close a gap — in distance, in work, or in news.
examples: Go on ahead; I'll catch up.
She was two laps down and never caught up.
I spent Sunday catching up on email.
We should catch up sometime — it's been a year.
He got caught up in the excitement and bid twice what he meant to.
Two of the clerks were caught up in the investigation.
She caught up her bag and ran for the gate.

senses.head: Reach someone ahead of you
examples: Go on ahead; I'll catch up.
She was two laps down and never caught up.

senses.head: Get current on work or sleep
examples: I spent Sunday catching up on email.

senses.head: Exchange news
body: A whole American social ritual lives in this sense. (поболтать, узнать новости друг о друге)
examples: We should catch up sometime — it's been a year.

senses.head: Be caught up in — absorbed or entangled
examples: He got caught up in the excitement and bid twice what he meant to.
Two of the clerks were caught up in the investigation.

senses.head: Snatch up quickly
body: Dated and literary; this is the one use that separates. (подхватить, схватить)
examples: She caught up her bag and ran for the gate.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on up; the noun catch-up keeps it there in play catch-up
entries.separable: mostly no — in the everyday senses it takes no object at all (run to catch up), and the person or work involved goes after with or on. There is one older transitive use, "snatch up," which does separate: catch up your coat, catch it up. British speakers also split it in the "reach" sense — I'll catch you up — where Americans say I'll catch up with you.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive in the common senses, transitive in the dated "snatch up" sense and in the passive be caught up in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense; closing a gap takes time and takes the progressive: I spent Sunday catching up.
entries.passive: restricted — nothing to passivize in the common intransitive senses (✗ was caught up by me for I'll catch up), but sense 4 exists only as a passive: two of the clerks were caught up in the investigation.
entries.see also: catch up on, catch up with, come along

entries.meaning: To do the part of something that has piled up while you were away from it.
examples: I need a weekend to catch up on sleep.
She caught up on six weeks of paperwork in two days.
We catch up on the show every Sunday night.
He has never caught up on the reading from that first semester.
There's a stack of it on my desk and I'll never catch up on it.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress sits on up, and on is unstressed
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. The object follows the whole phrase: catch up on sleep, catch up on it. ✗ catch sleep up on, ✗ catch up sleep on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the work is done over a stretch of time: she was catching up on six weeks of paperwork.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is possible but stiff (the paperwork was finally caught up on) and collapses with an agent: ✗ sleep was caught up on by me.
entries.see also: catch up, catch up with

entries.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you — and, said of consequences, to reach someone at last.
examples: He caught up with the leaders on the last hill.
Start walking and I'll catch up with you at the corner.
The lies caught up with him in the end.
Thirty years of smoking caught up with her all at once.
I caught up with my old roommate over lunch.

senses.head: Reach someone ahead of you
examples: He caught up with the leaders on the last hill.
Start walking and I'll catch up with you at the corner.

senses.head: (Of consequences) finally affect someone
body: The subject is the trouble, not the person. (настигнуть, дать о себе знать)
examples: The lies caught up with him in the end.
Thirty years of smoking caught up with her all at once.

senses.head: Meet and exchange news
examples: I caught up with my old roommate over lunch.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on up; both catch and with are unstressed
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: catch up with her, ✗ catch her up with, ✗ catch up her with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 2 personifies the trouble but is still an event: the lies caught up with him in the end.
entries.passive: no — ✗ he was caught up with by the leaders, ✗ he was caught up with by his lies. Keep it active.
entries.see also: catch up, catch out, come after

entries.meaning: To split a group into two teams by taking turns picking players; by extension, to take sides in a quarrel.
examples: We chose up sides and played until it got dark.
The kids choose up every recess without an adult anywhere near.
By Tuesday the whole department had chosen up sides.
Somebody has to choose up before we can start.
They chose up teams right there in the parking lot.
entries.русский: разбиваться на команды, выбирать игроков по очереди
entries.separable: no in practice — the only objects it takes are the fixed sides and teams, and neither moves: choose up sides, ✗ choose sides up.
entries.transitive: either — with sides, with teams, or with nothing at all
entries.register: everyday — American; a British speaker says pick teams
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a one-time act of dividing a group into teams.
entries.passive: restricted — sides were chosen up before anyone thought to argue passes, but an agent kills it: ✗ sides were chosen up by the kids.
entries.see also: come between, cut in

entries.meaning: To hold on tight, especially when you are close to losing your grip — on a rope, on a lead, or on a job.
examples: She clung on with both hands until the wave passed.
Cling on — the ladder shifts when you step off it.
He clung on to the rail all the way down the stairs.
The company has clung on through three bad quarters.
Their lead was one point, and they clung on for six more minutes.
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); with to it becomes a three-part verb
entries.separable: no — nothing goes between the two words, and what you are holding follows to: cling on to the rail, ✗ cling the rail on, ✗ cling on the rail to.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; add to to name what is being held
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but durative, an activity you keep doing: she was clinging on with both hands.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ the rail was clung on to.
entries.see also: cling to, catch on

entries.meaning: To hold on to something and refuse to let go, whether it is a rope, a belief, or a smell in a room.
examples: The kid clung to his mother's leg the whole time.
Two of them clung to the overturned hull until morning.
She clings to the idea that he'll call.
They clung to the old numbers long after everyone knew better.
The smoke clung to every coat in the closet.
That nickname clung to him for thirty years.

senses.head: Hold on physically
examples: The kid clung to his mother's leg the whole time.
Two of them clung to the overturned hull until morning.

senses.head: Refuse to give up a hope or a belief
examples: She clings to the idea that he'll call.
They clung to the old numbers long after everyone knew better.

senses.head: (Of a fabric, a smell, a reputation) stick to
examples: The smoke clung to every coat in the closet.
That nickname clung to him for thirty years.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, not a particle — the verb keeps the stress and to reduces to /tə/
entries.русский: цепляться за, держаться за, не расставаться с
entries.separable: no — the object always follows to: cling to the raft, never ✗ cling the raft to. With a pronoun it still follows: cling to it.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative in senses 1–2; sense 3 (a smell, a nickname) is closer to stative, a condition that simply lasts: that nickname clung to him for thirty years.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive fails: ✗ the raft was clung to, ✗ he was clung to by the nickname.
entries.see also: cling on, catch at, come between

entries.meaning: To happen, especially in a way that invites the question how.
examples: How did this whole arrangement come about?
The merger came about almost by accident.
Change like that comes about slowly or not at all.
Nobody can quite explain how the rumor came about.
She called the turn and the boat came about cleanly.

senses.head: Happen, come to pass
body: Nearly always with how, or in an explanation of how something happened. (происходить, случаться)
examples: How did this whole arrangement come about?
The merger came about almost by accident.
Change like that comes about slowly or not at all.
Nobody can quite explain how the rumor came about.

senses.head: (Sailing) turn through the wind onto a new tack
examples: She called the turn and the boat came about cleanly.

entries.separable: no — there is no object to move at all. ✗ come the change about, ✗ come it about.
entries.register: everyday — the sailing sense is specialized
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an event verb of happening, with no agent behind it: the merger came about almost by accident.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and like happen it will not passivize at all: ✗ the merger was come about.
entries.see also: come along, come up, come to

entries.meaning: To find something by chance, or to make a particular impression on other people.
examples: I came across an old photo of my grandfather in a shoebox.
She came across the discrepancy while closing the books.
If you come across it, hang on to it for me.
He comes across as arrogant, but he's just shy.
In the interview she came across very well.
They wouldn't ship until he came across with the deposit.
Come across with the rest of it and we're done.

senses.head: Find by chance
body: The thing found is not being looked for; that is the whole point of the verb. (натолкнуться на, случайно найти)
examples: I came across an old photo of my grandfather in a shoebox.
She came across the discrepancy while closing the books.
If you come across it, hang on to it for me.

senses.head: Come across (as) — give an impression
body: Followed by as plus an adjective or a noun phrase, or — with well and badly — by the adverb alone. (производить впечатление, казаться)
examples: He comes across as arrogant, but he's just shy.
In the interview she came across very well.

senses.head: Come across with — hand over what is owed
examples: They wouldn't ship until he came across with the deposit.
Come across with the rest of it and we're done.

entries.русский: натолкнуться на, случайно найти; производить впечатление
entries.type: prepositional verb in the "find" sense, phrasal verb in the "seem" sense
entries.separable: no — come across an old photo, never ✗ come an old photo across, and a pronoun stays put too: come across it.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you find something, intransitive when you make an impression
entries.register: everyday — the "hand over" sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1, a chance discovery; in sense 2 come across (as) behaves as a linking verb, joining subject to a complement — he comes across as arrogant, she came across very well.
entries.passive: no — the standard example of a prepositional verb that refuses the passive: ✗ an old photo was come across. Say was found instead.
entries.see also: come upon, come off, come over, come by

entries.meaning: To pursue someone with hostile intent — in person, in court, or in print. (The plain sequence sense, B comes after A, is literal and needs no entry.)
examples: If this gets out, they will come after you.
The label came after him for every dollar of the advance.
She knew the story would come after her sooner or later.
Two collection agencies came after the same debt.
Say that in public and his lawyers will come after the paper, not you.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress sits on the first syllable of after
entries.separable: no — the object always follows after: come after me, never ✗ come me after.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.register: everyday — informal in the sense of going after someone aggressively
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; pursuit with hostile intent, fine in the progressive: they're coming after you.
entries.passive: no — ✗ you will be come after by them; come does not passivize under a preposition.
entries.see also: come at, come down on, catch up with

entries.meaning: To accompany someone, to make progress, or to turn up when needed.
examples: We're going to the game — you should come along.
He came along mostly to see the house.
The garden is coming along nicely this year.
Her Spanish has come along faster than mine.
A job like that doesn't come along twice.
Wait ten minutes and another one comes along.

senses.head: Accompany, join in
body: Often as an invitation. (пойти вместе, увязаться)
examples: We're going to the game — you should come along.
He came along mostly to see the house.

senses.head: Progress, develop
body: Usually with nicely, well, or slowly. (продвигаться, налаживаться)
examples: The garden is coming along nicely this year.
Her Spanish has come along faster than mine.

senses.head: Turn up, become available
body: Of chances, buses, and people. (подвернуться, появиться)
examples: A job like that doesn't come along twice.
Wait ten minutes and another one comes along.

entries.русский: идти вместе, увязаться; продвигаться, налаживаться; подвернуться
entries.separable: no — intransitive in all three senses, so there is nothing to place. ✗ come the kids along.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — accompanying, progressing (the garden is coming along nicely), and turning up.
entries.passive: no — intransitive throughout; ✗ the kids were come along.
entries.see also: come around, come up, catch up

entries.meaning: To fall to pieces, whether the thing is a chair, a deal, or a person.
examples: The binding came apart the second time I opened it.
Two of the shelves came apart in the move.
The case came apart once the witness changed her story.
He came apart on the stand.
By August the whole coalition was coming apart at the seams.

senses.head: Fall to pieces physically
examples: The binding came apart the second time I opened it.
Two of the shelves came apart in the move.

senses.head: (Of a plan, a marriage, a person) break down
body: Often come apart at the seams. (рушиться, расклеиться)
examples: The case came apart once the witness changed her story.
He came apart on the stand.
By August the whole coalition was coming apart at the seams.

entries.separable: no — intransitive; the thing that falls apart is the subject, not an object. ✗ come the chair apart.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state with the thing itself as subject: the binding came apart, he came apart on the stand.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the subject is already the affected thing, so a passive has nothing to promote: ✗ the binding was come apart.
entries.see also: come off, come away, come together

entries.meaning: To regain consciousness, to change your mind at last, to drop by, or to roll around again.
examples: She came around in the ambulance and asked about the dog.
Give him a week and he'll come around.
The committee finally came around to her proposal.
He comes around every couple of weeks with the rent.
Tax season comes around whether you're ready or not.
When the anniversary came around, nobody mentioned it.

senses.head: Regain consciousness
examples: She came around in the ambulance and asked about the dog.

senses.head: Change your mind, be won over
body: Usually come around to. (согласиться, переменить мнение)
examples: Give him a week and he'll come around.
The committee finally came around to her proposal.

senses.head: Drop by, visit
examples: He comes around every couple of weeks with the rent.

senses.head: Come again in its turn
examples: Tax season comes around whether you're ready or not.
When the anniversary came around, nobody mentioned it.

entries.русский: прийти в себя, очнуться; согласиться, изменить мнение; зайти в гости; снова наступить
entries.separable: no — intransitive; when a person or an opinion is named, it follows a preposition: come around to my way of thinking.
entries.register: everyday — American; British speakers say come round
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses; each is a change or an event, never a state.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ her proposal was come around to.
entries.see also: come round, come to, come by, come over

entries.meaning: To rush at someone, or to approach a problem from a particular direction.
examples: He came at me with a tire iron.
Questions came at her from every side of the room.
Let's come at this from the other end.
If you come at the proof that way, it collapses.
That kind of speed comes at a price.

senses.head: Rush at, attack
examples: He came at me with a tire iron.
Questions came at her from every side of the room.

senses.head: Approach a problem from an angle
examples: Let's come at this from the other end.
If you come at the proof that way, it collapses.

senses.head: Come at a price — have a cost attached
body: A fixed pattern. (обходиться дорого, доставаться ценой)
examples: That kind of speed comes at a price.

entries.pronunciation note: unusually for a preposition, at takes the stress here
entries.separable: no — the object always follows at: came at me, never ✗ came me at.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1–2, an attack or an angle of approach; the fixed come at a price in sense 3 is stative — it means cost, not move.
entries.passive: no — ✗ I was come at with a tire iron; only the active works.
entries.see also: come after, come up against, come down on

entries.meaning: To leave a place or an event carrying something — usually an impression — or, of a part, to detach itself.
examples: I came away with the feeling that he hadn't read it.
She came away from the meeting convinced it was a mistake.
They came away with two medals and a broken van.
The handle came away in my hand.
Whole sheets of wallpaper came away when the heat was on.

senses.head: Leave with an impression or a result
body: Almost always with with or feeling. (уйти с ощущением, вынести (впечатление))
examples: I came away with the feeling that he hadn't read it.
She came away from the meeting convinced it was a mistake.
They came away with two medals and a broken van.

senses.head: Become detached
examples: The handle came away in my hand.
Whole sheets of wallpaper came away when the heat was on.

entries.separable: no — intransitive; what you take away with you follows with. ✗ come the impression away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: leaving with an impression (sense 1), or a part detaching itself (sense 2).
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ the handle was come away, ✗ the feeling was come away with.
entries.see also: come off, come apart, come out

entries.meaning: To return — to a place, to popularity, to memory, or with a retort.
examples: He came back three days later as if nothing had happened.
Wide legs came back about five years ago.
They were down eighteen and came back to win.
It'll come back to me in a minute.
The tune came back to her halfway through dinner.
She came back at him with the actual numbers.
He had nothing to come back with.

senses.head: Return
examples: He came back three days later as if nothing had happened.

senses.head: Return to popularity or into contention
examples: Wide legs came back about five years ago.
They were down eighteen and came back to win.

senses.head: Come back to someone — be remembered
body: The memory is the subject. (вспоминаться, всплывать в памяти)
examples: It'll come back to me in a minute.
The tune came back to her halfway through dinner.

senses.head: Come back at someone — retort
examples: She came back at him with the actual numbers.
He had nothing to come back with.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on back; the noun comeback moves it to come
entries.русский: вернуться; снова войти в моду; вспомниться; огрызнуться
entries.separable: no — intransitive; a person or thing involved follows a preposition: come back to me, come back at him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses, including sense 3, where the memory is the subject: the tune came back to her halfway through dinner.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ he was come back at by her.
entries.see also: come around, come to, come out with

entries.meaning: To damage the relationship between two people, or to interfere with something someone cares about.
examples: Money came between the two brothers for good.
I won't let this come between us.
Nothing comes between that man and his Saturday.
Her family came between them within a year.
Don't let a scheduling mix-up come between you and a good hire.
entries.separable: no — the two people always follow between: come between us, never ✗ come us between.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an event that damages a relationship, though the generic present reads almost stative: nothing comes between that man and his Saturday.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the two brothers were come between by money.
entries.see also: come after, cut in, cling to

entries.meaning: To stop in briefly, or to get hold of something.
examples: Come by the office any time before five.
She came by with soup and left again in ten minutes.
Parts for that model are hard to come by.
How did he come by a key to the building?
She came by the house through her aunt.

senses.head: Drop by, visit briefly
examples: Come by the office any time before five.
She came by with soup and left again in ten minutes.

senses.head: Obtain, get hold of
body: Most often in hard to come by and in questions about how something was got. (раздобыть, заполучить)
examples: Parts for that model are hard to come by.
How did he come by a key to the building?
She came by the house through her aunt.

entries.type: phrasal verb in the "visit" sense, prepositional verb in the "obtain" sense
entries.separable: no — in the "obtain" sense the object always follows by: come by a good job, ✗ come a good job by, ✗ come it by.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you obtain something, intransitive when you drop in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: a brief visit (sense 1) and an act of obtaining (sense 2).
entries.passive: no — ✗ a key to the building was come by. The fixed hard to come by is an infinitive, not a passive: parts for that model are hard to come by.
entries.see also: come across, come around, come into, come upon

entries.meaning: To fall — in price, from an older generation, or physically — and, informally, to descend from a high.
examples: Prices have come down about twenty percent since spring.
The swelling should come down overnight.
The recipe came down through her mother's side.
Only two of the letters have come down to us.
The old grandstand came down in a morning.
He was still coming down when the sun came up.

senses.head: Decrease, fall (of prices, fever, swelling)
examples: Prices have come down about twenty percent since spring.
The swelling should come down overnight.

senses.head: Be handed down from the past
body: Usually come down to us. (доходить, передаваться)
examples: The recipe came down through her mother's side.
Only two of the letters have come down to us.

senses.head: Collapse, be demolished
examples: The old grandstand came down in a morning.

senses.head: Descend from a drug high
examples: He was still coming down when the sun came up.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on down; the noun comedown moves it to come
entries.русский: снижаться (о ценах); передаваться (из поколения в поколение); рухнуть; отходить (после наркотика)
entries.separable: no — intransitive; anything further is added by a preposition, giving the three-part verbs come down on, come down to, and come down with.
entries.register: everyday — the drug sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a fall in price, a handing-down, a collapse — all changes over time: prices have come down about twenty percent.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ the old grandstand was come down.
entries.see also: come down on, come down to, come down with, cast down

entries.meaning: To punish or criticize someone severely.
examples: The league came down on the team with a record fine.
His editor came down on him hard for that paragraph.
Don't come down on her — she wasn't even here.
The city has come down on short-term rentals all year.
If they catch it in the audit, they'll come down on us for the whole quarter.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress is on down; on is weak
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: came down on him, ✗ came him down on. Only an adverb like hard may sit before on: came down hard on him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of punishment or criticism, often with hard.
entries.passive: no — unlike look down on, this one will not passivize: ✗ he was come down on hard by his editor. Recast as active.
entries.see also: come down, come after, come in for

entries.meaning: To be, when everything else is stripped away, a matter of one thing. Often in the fixed when it comes down to it.
examples: It all comes down to money in the end.
The choice came down to two candidates.
When it comes down to it, nobody wants to be the one who says no.
Everything has come down to whether the permit clears by Friday.
If it comes down to his word against hers, we lose.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on down, with to reduced to /tə/
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: comes down to money, ✗ comes money down to.
entries.verb type: stative — it means amount to, not move, and resists the progressive: ✗ it is coming down to money.
entries.passive: no — stative and unaccusative at once: ✗ money is come down to by it.
entries.see also: come down, come to, come out

entries.meaning: To start to have an illness — and, by long habit, a minor one. You come down with a cold or the flu; you do not come down with cancer.
examples: Half the class came down with strep the same week.
I think I'm coming down with something.
She came down with the flu two days before the wedding.
He has come down with whatever the twins had.
If you come down with it, stay home.
entries.separable: no — the illness always follows the whole phrase: came down with the flu, ✗ came the flu down with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state you can be in the middle of: I think I'm coming down with something.
entries.passive: no — ✗ strep was come down with by half the class.
entries.see also: come down, come over, creep up on

entries.meaning: To present yourself voluntarily, especially to give evidence or to claim something.
examples: Three witnesses came forward after the appeal.
Nobody has come forward to claim the money.
She came forward with the emails a year later.
Police are asking anyone who saw the truck to come forward.
He would not come forward while his boss still worked there.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the first syllable of forward
entries.separable: no — intransitive; what you offer follows with: come forward with information.
entries.register: everyday — very common in news writing
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a voluntary act, normally reported as a single event.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; ✗ the emails were come forward with.
entries.see also: come out, come out with, come through

entries.meaning: To have a place, a family, or a source as your origin.
examples: Both of her grandparents come from Ohio.
He comes from a family of teachers.
The money came from a small family trust.
That smell is coming from under the sink.
I see where you're coming from, but the budget won't stretch.
Once you know he grew up there, you see where the argument comes from.

senses.head: Have as a hometown or background
body: Stays in the simple present even about someone long dead. (быть родом из)
examples: Both of her grandparents come from Ohio.
He comes from a family of teachers.

senses.head: Have as a source or cause
examples: The money came from a small family trust.
That smell is coming from under the sink.

senses.head: See where someone is coming from — understand their position
body: Informal and fixed. (понимать, откуда человек исходит)
examples: I see where you're coming from, but the budget won't stretch.
Once you know he grew up there, you see where the argument comes from.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, not a particle — the verb keeps the stress and from weakens to /frəm/
entries.русский: быть родом из; происходить из; исходить от
entries.separable: no — the object always follows from: comes from Ohio, never ✗ comes Ohio from.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: stative in senses 1–2 — origin, not motion, and it stays in the simple present even of someone long dead: he comes from a family of teachers, ✗ he is coming from Ohio in that sense. A live source allows the progressive: that smell is coming from under the sink.
entries.passive: no — stative and prepositional both: ✗ Ohio is come from by her grandparents.
entries.see also: come out, come into, come by

entries.meaning: Beyond the literal "enter," a cluster of senses about arriving, finishing, and being useful.
examples: The first returns came in just after nine.
Not much is coming in this quarter.
She came in third and set a personal best.
Peaches come in around the end of June.
Bell-bottoms came in twice in one lifetime.
Keep the box; it'll come in handy.
That second key came in handy the night I locked myself out.

senses.head: Arrive, be received (of money, results, reports)
examples: The first returns came in just after nine.
Not much is coming in this quarter.

senses.head: Finish in a position
examples: She came in third and set a personal best.

senses.head: Become available or fashionable
examples: Peaches come in around the end of June.
Bell-bottoms came in twice in one lifetime.

senses.head: Come in handy — turn out to be useful
examples: Keep the box; it'll come in handy.
That second key came in handy the night I locked myself out.

entries.русский: поступать (о деньгах, данных); прийти (в забеге); войти в моду; пригодиться
entries.separable: no — intransitive; anything more is added by a preposition, as in come in for criticism. ✗ come the money in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — arriving, finishing a race, becoming fashionable: not much is coming in this quarter.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; and come in handy takes an adjective, not an object: ✗ it was come in handy.
entries.see also: come in for, come into, come out

entries.meaning: To receive something directed at you, usually unwelcome.
examples: The mayor came in for heavy criticism over the contract.
The design has come in for praise from an unexpected quarter.
Their hiring practices came in for scrutiny after the lawsuit.
He came in for his share of the blame.
Any policy that raises fares will come in for it from riders.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on in; for reduces to /fər/
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: came in for criticism, ✗ came criticism in for.
entries.register: formal — mainly journalism; the object is nearly always criticism, blame, scrutiny, or praise
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an event of receiving something aimed at you (the mayor came in for heavy criticism); the progressive is fine: the plan is coming in for criticism from both sides.
entries.passive: no. The object is a fixed idiomatic noun (criticism, blame, scrutiny, praise) that cannot be promoted: ✗ heavy criticism was come in for by the mayor. The phrase is already the receiving end — for a passive, switch verbs: the mayor was criticized.
entries.see also: come down on, come under, come in

entries.meaning: To acquire something suddenly, usually by inheritance, or to enter a state.
examples: He came into a little money when his uncle died.
She came into the farm and the debts along with it.
The new rules come into effect on the first.
The coast came into view about an hour out.
Other factors come into play once the loan is approved.

senses.head: Inherit, acquire suddenly
examples: He came into a little money when his uncle died.
She came into the farm and the debts along with it.

senses.head: Enter a state or condition
body: A short fixed list: come into effect, into force, into view, into fashion, into play, into being. (вступать в, входить в)
examples: The new rules come into effect on the first.
The coast came into view about an hour out.
Other factors come into play once the loan is approved.

entries.русский: получить в наследство, неожиданно получить; вступить (в силу), войти (в моду, в поле зрения)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows into: came into money, never ✗ came money into.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the sudden acquiring (he came into a little money) and the entering of a state (the rules come into effect on the first). Progressive fine: the new fee is coming into effect next month.
entries.passive: no. A prepositional verb whose object never moves to subject: ✗ a little money was come into by him, ✗ effect was come into by the rules. Say he inherited the money / the rules took effect.
entries.see also: come in, come by, come under

entries.meaning: To detach, to succeed, to give an impression, or to be fresh from something.
examples: The knob came off in my hand.
The stain came off with plain soap.
The surprise party almost didn't come off.
It was an ambitious pitch, and it came off.
He comes off as colder than he is.
They're coming off three straight wins.
Come off it — you were asleep by ten.

senses.head: Become detached
examples: The knob came off in my hand.
The stain came off with plain soap.

senses.head: Succeed, work out
examples: The surprise party almost didn't come off.
It was an ambitious pitch, and it came off.

senses.head: Come off as — give an impression
body: The American form; British speakers say come over as. (производить впечатление, казаться)
examples: He comes off as colder than he is.

senses.head: Be fresh from a period or a place
examples: They're coming off three straight wins.

senses.head: Come off it — I don't believe you
body: Informal, always as an imperative. (да брось, не заливай)
examples: Come off it — you were asleep by ten.

entries.русский: отвалиться, отойти; удаться, получиться; производить впечатление
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional when a place or period follows
entries.separable: no — nothing sits between come and off. When off takes an object it is a preposition and the object follows: come off the bench, ✗ come the bench off.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive in the main senses, prepositional in come off a win
entries.register: everyday — come off it is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the detaching (the knob came off), succeeding (the party almost didn't come off), and fresh-from senses (they're coming off three straight wins). Come off as is linking (copular): what follows describes the subject, not an object — he comes off as colder than he is.
entries.passive: no. Senses 1–2 are intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the stain was come off. The prepositional uses refuse it too: ✗ the bench was come off, ✗ three straight wins are being come off.
entries.see also: come across, come over, come apart, come away

entries.meaning: To start working, start happening, or take the stage — plus the most-used interjection in American English.
examples: Come on, we're going to miss the first inning.
Oh, come on — nobody believes that.
The porch light comes on at dusk.
The heat hadn't come on yet and the office was freezing.
I feel a headache coming on.
The rain came on just as we reached the car.
She comes on right after the intermission.

senses.head: Come on! — hurry up, or you can't be serious
body: Informal, and the tone does all the work. (давай, ну же; да брось)
examples: Come on, we're going to miss the first inning.
Oh, come on — nobody believes that.

senses.head: Start working (of lights, heat, power)
examples: The porch light comes on at dusk.
The heat hadn't come on yet and the office was freezing.

senses.head: Begin (of illness or weather)
examples: I feel a headache coming on.
The rain came on just as we reached the car.

senses.head: Take the stage, enter the game
examples: She comes on right after the intermission.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on on; the noun come-on keeps it on come
entries.русский: давай, ну же; включаться (о свете); начинаться (о болезни); выходить (на сцену)
entries.separable: no — intransitive throughout; the person addressed is not an object. ✗ come the lights on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: a light or a heater starting (the porch light comes on at dusk), an illness or weather beginning (I feel a headache coming on), an actor entering (she comes on after the intermission). Come on! is a fixed interjection with no tense or aspect of its own.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in every sense, so no passive exists: ✗ the heat was come on, ✗ the stage was come on by her.
entries.see also: come on to, come out, creep up

entries.meaning: To make an unmistakable sexual advance to someone.
examples: He came on to her at the office party and she left early.
She came on to him so hard that the whole table noticed.
Nobody wants to be come on to by a manager.
If a customer comes on to you, tell a supervisor.
He swears he wasn't coming on to anyone.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on on, with to reduced
entries.separable: no — the person follows the whole phrase: came on to her, ✗ came her on to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate act, and the progressive is normal: he swears he wasn't coming on to anyone.
entries.passive: yes — one of the few come phrasals that passivizes cleanly, because the object is a person: nobody wants to be come on to by a manager, she'd been come on to twice that night.
entries.see also: come on, come across

entries.meaning: To become public, to be released, to be removed, or to turn out a certain way.
examples: The book comes out in March.
The truth came out at the second hearing.
It came out that he had never held the license.
Red wine won't come out of linen.
He came out to his family at nineteen.
None of the pictures came out.
She came out of it better than anyone expected.

senses.head: Be published or released
examples: The book comes out in March.

senses.head: Become known
examples: The truth came out at the second hearing.
It came out that he had never held the license.

senses.head: Be removed (of stains, teeth, screws)
examples: Red wine won't come out of linen.

senses.head: Publicly identify as gay, lesbian, bisexual, or trans
body: From come out of the closet. (совершить каминг-аут)
examples: He came out to his family at nineteen.

senses.head: Turn out, end up
body: Of photographs, results, and people. (получаться, выходить)
examples: None of the pictures came out.
She came out of it better than anyone expected.

entries.русский: выйти (о книге, фильме); выясниться, всплыть; отстирываться; совершить каминг-аут; получиться (о фото)
entries.separable: no — intransitive; what is revealed or released is the subject, not an object. ✗ come the truth out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: being released (the book comes out in March), becoming known (the truth came out), being removed (red wine won't come out of linen), coming out publicly (he came out at nineteen). Sense 5 shades into linking, with an adjective describing the subject: none of the pictures came out well.
entries.passive: no — intransitive throughout; what is revealed or released is already the subject: ✗ the truth was come out, ✗ the book has been come out in March. Use be published, be revealed.
entries.see also: come out with, come forward, come off, come through

entries.meaning: To say something startling, or to put a new product on the market.
examples: Then he came out with the strangest question I've ever been asked.
She came out with the whole story before anyone could stop her.
They come out with a new version every fall.
The company has come out with a cheaper model.
If nobody comes out with a fix, we'll write our own.

senses.head: Say something abruptly or surprisingly
examples: Then he came out with the strangest question I've ever been asked.
She came out with the whole story before anyone could stop her.

senses.head: Release a new product
examples: They come out with a new version every fall.
The company has come out with a cheaper model.
If nobody comes out with a fix, we'll write our own.

entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: came out with a new model, ✗ came a new model out with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the blurting (then he came out with the strangest question) and the releasing (they come out with a new version every fall); progressive fine: they're coming out with a cheaper model.
entries.passive: no in practice. The three-part passive is unusable here: ✗ a cheaper model has been come out with, ✗ the whole story was come out with. Switch verbs: a cheaper model has been released.
entries.see also: come out, come up with

entries.meaning: To visit someone at home, or (of a feeling) to take hold of a person.
examples: Come over Saturday and we'll grill something.
Her parents came over for coffee and stayed four hours.
A wave of dizziness came over him on the stairs.
I don't know what came over me.
In print he comes over as rather severe.

senses.head: Visit, come to someone's house
examples: Come over Saturday and we'll grill something.
Her parents came over for coffee and stayed four hours.

senses.head: (Of a feeling) affect someone suddenly
body: Most often in what has come over you? (находить на кого-л., охватывать)
examples: A wave of dizziness came over him on the stairs.
I don't know what came over me.

senses.head: Come over as — give an impression
body: British; Americans say come off as or come across as. (производить впечатление)
examples: In print he comes over as rather severe.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the first syllable of over
entries.русский: зайти, заглянуть; найти на кого-то (о чувстве)
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional when a person follows
entries.separable: no — in the "affect" sense the person follows over: came over me, never ✗ came me over.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive when you visit, transitive when a feeling affects someone
entries.register: everyday — the come over as sense is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the visiting sense (her parents came over for coffee) and in the seizing-feeling sense (a wave of dizziness came over him). The British come over as is linking: in print he comes over as rather severe.
entries.passive: no. Sense 1 is intransitive (✗ my house was come over), and the feeling sense refuses promotion even though a person follows: ✗ he was come over by a wave of dizziness, ✗ I was come over by something.
entries.see also: come by, come around, come off, come across

entries.meaning: The British form of come around: to regain consciousness, to be won over, to drop by, or to come again in its turn.
examples: She came round about ten minutes after the anesthetic wore off.
Give him time and he'll come round to the idea.
Come round on Sunday if you're free.
Exam season comes round faster every year.
She said she'd come round after work with the paint.
entries.русский: прийти в себя; согласиться; зайти; снова наступить
entries.separable: no — intransitive, exactly like come around.
entries.register: British — the standard American form is come around, in every one of these senses
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: regaining consciousness (she came round ten minutes later), being won over (he'll come round to the idea), dropping by, and recurring (exam season comes round faster every year).
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no passive at all: ✗ she was come round after the anesthetic, ✗ the idea was come round to.
entries.see also: come around, come to

entries.meaning: To deliver what you promised, to survive something, or (of paperwork) to be approved at last.
examples: He came through with the money on the last day.
She has come through for us every single time.
They came through the fire with the house standing.
He came through the surgery fine.
The visa finally came through in April.
If the transfer comes through today, we can close.

senses.head: Deliver, do what was needed
body: Often come through for someone. (не подвести, справиться)
examples: He came through with the money on the last day.
She has come through for us every single time.

senses.head: Survive, get past
examples: They came through the fire with the house standing.
He came through the surgery fine.

senses.head: (Of paperwork, permits, messages) arrive or be approved
examples: The visa finally came through in April.
If the transfer comes through today, we can close.

entries.русский: не подвести, справиться; пережить, выкарабкаться; пройти (о документах)
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional when a thing survived follows
entries.separable: no — nothing goes between the words; what you survived follows through: came through the surgery, ✗ came the surgery through.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive in the "deliver" sense, prepositional in the "survive" sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: delivering (he came through with the money), surviving (he came through the surgery fine), and paperwork being approved (the visa finally came through). Progressive fine: if the transfer is coming through today, we can close.
entries.passive: no. Sense 1 and sense 3 are intransitive (✗ the money was come through with), and the survive sense resists the prepositional passive: ✗ the surgery was come through, ✗ the fire was come through by the family.
entries.see also: come out, come forward, cut through

entries.meaning: To regain consciousness; to add up to; to reach a point or a person.
examples: He came to on the kitchen floor with no idea how long he'd been there.
The bill came to forty-two dollars with tip.
Repairs have come to more than the car is worth.
I hope it doesn't come to a lawsuit.
The name came to me in the shower.
Come to think of it, she never answered the question.

senses.head: Regain consciousness
examples: He came to on the kitchen floor with no idea how long he'd been there.

senses.head: Add up to, amount to
examples: The bill came to forty-two dollars with tip.
Repairs have come to more than the car is worth.

senses.head: Reach a state or a point
body: Often in it never came to that. (дойти до)
examples: I hope it doesn't come to a lawsuit.

senses.head: Come to someone — occur to, be remembered
examples: The name came to me in the shower.
Come to think of it, she never answered the question.

entries.pronunciation note: in the "regain consciousness" sense to is a stressed particle and keeps its full /tu/; elsewhere it is a preposition and weakens to /tə/
entries.русский: очнуться, прийти в себя; составить (сумму); дойти до (чего-л.)
entries.type: phrasal verb in the "revive" sense, prepositional verb elsewhere
entries.separable: no — in the "revive" sense there is no object at all; everywhere else the object follows to: came to forty dollars, ✗ came forty dollars to.
entries.verb type: Both. Sense 1 is action — dynamic and intransitive: he came to on the kitchen floor. Sense 2 (amount to) is stative, like cost, and rejects the progressive: ✗ the bill is coming to forty-two dollars. Senses 3–4 are dynamic again: I hope it doesn't come to a lawsuit, the name came to me in the shower.
entries.passive: no. Sense 1 has no object at all. The stative amount sense refuses the passive the way cost does: ✗ forty-two dollars was come to by the bill; so does the occur-to sense: ✗ I was come to by the name.
entries.see also: come around, come down to, come up

entries.meaning: To assemble, or (of a plan or a piece of work) to start finally working as a whole.
examples: The town came together after the flood.
Two families came together over one long table.
The album came together in about three weeks.
It looked hopeless in June and then it all came together.
Give the sauce a minute and it comes together.

senses.head: Assemble, unite
examples: The town came together after the flood.
Two families came together over one long table.

senses.head: Take shape, work out
examples: The album came together in about three weeks.
It looked hopeless in June and then it all came together.
Give the sauce a minute and it comes together.

entries.separable: no — intransitive; the people or parts are the subject. ✗ come the town together.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, people assembling (the town came together after the flood) and a plan taking shape (the album came together in about three weeks); progressive normal: it's finally coming together.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the people or the parts are the subject already: ✗ the town was come together, ✗ the album has been come together.
entries.see also: come apart, come along, come off

entries.meaning: To fall within a category or authority, or to be subjected to attack or pressure.
examples: Rentals under thirty days come under a different ordinance.
That whole department comes under the state, not the city.
The proposal came under fire from both parties.
Her records came under review after the complaint.
The bridge design has come under fresh criticism this month.

senses.head: Fall within a category or jurisdiction
examples: Rentals under thirty days come under a different ordinance.
That whole department comes under the state, not the city.

senses.head: Be subjected to attack, pressure, or scrutiny
examples: The proposal came under fire from both parties.
Her records came under review after the complaint.
The bridge design has come under fresh criticism this month.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the first syllable of under
entries.separable: no — the object always follows under: came under fire, never ✗ came fire under.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: Both. Sense 1 (fall within a category or jurisdiction) is stative — a standing relationship, awkward in the progressive: ✗ that department is coming under the state. Sense 2 is action — dynamic: the proposal came under fire from both parties.
entries.passive: no. A prepositional verb whose object is a fixed noun that cannot be promoted: ✗ fire was come under by the proposal, ✗ a different ordinance is come under by short rentals. For the passive idea use was criticized, was reviewed.
entries.see also: come in for, come down on, come into

entries.meaning: To arise, to approach, or to be nearly here.
examples: Her name came up twice in the meeting.
Something came up and I had to cancel.
A stranger came up to me on the platform.
Finals are coming up fast.
His review comes up in October.
The tulips came up early this year.
The sun came up before we'd finished loading.

senses.head: Arise, be raised (of a subject or a problem)
examples: Her name came up twice in the meeting.
Something came up and I had to cancel.

senses.head: Approach someone
examples: A stranger came up to me on the platform.

senses.head: Be nearly here (of an event or a date)
examples: Finals are coming up fast.
His review comes up in October.

senses.head: Rise (of the sun, plants, water)
examples: The tulips came up early this year.
The sun came up before we'd finished loading.

entries.русский: возникнуть, всплыть (о вопросе); подойти; приближаться (о событии); взойти
entries.separable: no — intransitive; further material is added by a preposition, giving come up with and come up against. ✗ come the question up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: a topic arising (her name came up twice), approaching someone (a stranger came up to me), an event nearing (finals are coming up fast), and rising (the sun came up).
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the topic or the sun is the subject, never an object: ✗ her name was come up, ✗ I was come up to by a stranger.
entries.see also: come up with, come up against, come about, creep up

entries.meaning: To meet an obstacle or an opponent you cannot simply walk past.
examples: The bill came up against opposition in its own party.
We came up against the same permit problem twice.
She has come up against worse than a bad review.
Every startup comes up against this wall at about year three.
If you come up against anything you can't handle, call me.
entries.pronunciation note: the main stress is on up
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: came up against a wall, ✗ came a wall up against.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an event of meeting resistance, and the progressive is fine: we're coming up against the same permit problem again.
entries.passive: no in practice — the three-part passive is not used: ✗ the same permit problem was come up against twice, ✗ opposition was come up against by the bill. Rephrase with meet or run into.
entries.see also: come up, come at, come under

entries.meaning: To produce something on demand — an idea, an answer, or the money.
examples: She came up with the name in about four seconds.
Nobody could come up with a better explanation.
If you come up with something, send it over.
They had to come up with six thousand by Friday.
He came up with the deposit somehow.

senses.head: Produce an idea or an answer
examples: She came up with the name in about four seconds.
Nobody could come up with a better explanation.
If you come up with something, send it over.

senses.head: Produce money that is required
examples: They had to come up with six thousand by Friday.
He came up with the deposit somehow.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on up; come and with are both unstressed
entries.separable: no — nothing moves, not even a pronoun: come up with it. ✗ come a plan up with, ✗ come up a plan with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, producing an idea (she came up with the name in four seconds) and producing money (they had to come up with six thousand by Friday); progressive normal: he's coming up with excuses.
entries.passive: restricted. Possible but clumsy, and only with a light subject and no by-phrase: no better explanation was ever come up with. Avoid it with an agent — ✗ the name was come up with by her — and never in the money sense: ✗ six thousand had to be come up with.
entries.see also: come out with, come up, cast about

entries.meaning: To find something unexpectedly; in older writing, of a feeling, to take hold of someone.
examples: We came upon a clearing with a stone chimney still standing.
She came upon the letters while clearing out the attic.
He came upon them arguing in the hallway.
A great weariness came upon him.
Winter came upon the valley three weeks early.

senses.head: Find by chance
examples: We came upon a clearing with a stone chimney still standing.
She came upon the letters while clearing out the attic.
He came upon them arguing in the hallway.

senses.head: (Of a feeling or a season) overtake someone
examples: A great weariness came upon him.
Winter came upon the valley three weeks early.

entries.русский: наткнуться на, набрести на; охватить (о чувстве)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows upon: came upon a clearing, never ✗ came a clearing upon.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.register: formal — literary; the everyday American equivalent is come across
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a chance discovery (she came upon the letters in the attic) or, in literary use, a feeling or a season overtaking someone (a great weariness came upon him). Not progressive-friendly in the discovery sense, since the event is instantaneous.
entries.passive: restricted, and rare enough to avoid. The literary discovery sense is occasionally passivized (the cache was come upon by hikers), but ✗ the letters were come upon by her is poor, and the feeling sense refuses it outright: ✗ he was come upon by a great weariness.
entries.see also: come across, come by, creep up on

entries.meaning: To work out in detail what something will cost, item by item. Note the past tense: in this sense the verb is regular — we costed it out — even though plain cost never changes.
examples: Have the contractor cost out both options before we decide.
Finance costed the whole program out at nine million.
We costed it out twice and got two different numbers.
Nobody has costed out the maintenance, only the build.
Once you cost the labor out, the cheaper material stops being cheaper.
entries.separable: yes — cost out the renovation, cost the renovation out, and with a pronoun it must split: cost it out, never ✗ cost out it.
entries.register: formal — business, construction, and government budgeting
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a piece of work carried out on a budget, with the progressive fine: finance is costing out both options this week. Note the regular past in this sense — we costed it out — unlike plain stative cost, which never changes and rejects the progressive.
entries.passive: yes, and common in business writing: the maintenance has never been costed out, the whole program was costed out at nine million.
entries.see also: cut back, come to

entries.meaning: To appear slowly and unnoticed, said of things nobody wanted: errors, doubt, a tone of voice.
examples: Small errors creep in whenever the data is retyped.
A note of impatience crept in toward the end of the call.
Doubt had crept in long before she said anything.
Typos creep into every edition no matter how many people read it.
Let one exception creep in and the rule is gone.
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); with into it becomes prepositional
entries.separable: no — the thing that creeps in is the subject, not an object. ✗ creep errors in. To name the place, use into: errors crept into the data.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a slow unnoticed arrival: small errors creep in whenever the data is retyped, a note of impatience crept in toward the end. Progressive fine: doubt was creeping in.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the errors or the doubt are the subject: ✗ errors are crept in. The into variant resists the prepositional passive too: ✗ every edition is crept into by typos.
entries.see also: creep up, come in

entries.meaning: To give someone the creeps, or to leave a place quietly.
examples: That whole street creeps me out after dark.
The doll creeped out every kid at the party.
The soundtrack alone creeped half the theater out.
His questions creeped her out enough that she left.
He crept out at four in the morning without waking anyone.
Two of them crept out the side door during the speeches.

senses.head: Unnerve, give someone the creeps
body: Note the past tense: this sense is regular — creeped me out — while the literal verb keeps crept. (пугать, вызывать мурашки)
examples: That whole street creeps me out after dark.
The doll creeped out every kid at the party.
The soundtrack alone creeped half the theater out.
His questions creeped her out enough that she left.

senses.head: Leave quietly, slip away
body: Here the verb is irregular: crept out. (выскользнуть, тихонько уйти)
examples: He crept out at four in the morning without waking anyone.
Two of them crept out the side door during the speeches.

entries.separable: yes in the "unnerve" sense — the mask creeped out the kids, creeped the kids out, and with a pronoun it must split: it creeps me out, never ✗ it creeps out me. The "slip away" sense takes no object at all.
entries.register: informal — American; the "unnerve" sense is recent and still conversational
entries.verb type: Both. Sense 1 is action — dynamic and causative, a thing producing a feeling in someone: that street creeps me out after dark. Sense 2 is action — dynamic and intransitive: he crept out at four in the morning. Note the split past: regular creeped in sense 1, irregular crept in sense 2.
entries.passive: yes in the unnerve sense, and very common: I was completely creeped out by the doll, half the theater got creeped out by the soundtrack. No passive of the slip-away sense — it has no object: ✗ the side door was crept out.
entries.see also: creep in, creep up on

entries.meaning: To approach quietly, or to rise by small unnoticed amounts.
examples: Don't creep up behind me like that.
Rents have crept up every year since we moved in.
His blood pressure crept up over the winter.
The estimate creeps up a little each time they revise it.
Costs crept up so gradually that nobody flagged them.

senses.head: Approach quietly
examples: Don't creep up behind me like that.

senses.head: Rise slowly (of prices, numbers, temperature)
examples: Rents have crept up every year since we moved in.
His blood pressure crept up over the winter.
The estimate creeps up a little each time they revise it.
Costs crept up so gradually that nobody flagged them.

entries.русский: подкрадываться; медленно ползти вверх (о ценах, показателях)
entries.separable: no — intransitive; the person approached follows on, giving the three-part creep up on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, approaching quietly (don't creep up behind me) and rising by small amounts (rents have crept up every year); progressive fine: costs were creeping up all winter.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses: ✗ I was crept up behind, ✗ the estimate is crept up.
entries.see also: creep up on, come up, creep in

entries.meaning: To approach someone quietly from behind — and, said of time, deadlines, and age, to arrive before you noticed.
examples: The cat crept up on the bird and missed by a foot.
Don't creep up on people in a parking garage.
Fifty crept up on him faster than he'd planned for.
The deadline has crept up on us again.
It creeps up on you — one season you're fine, the next you need reading glasses.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress is on up; on is weak
entries.русский: подкрасться к; подкрасться незаметно (о времени, возрасте)
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: crept up on him, ✗ crept him up on, ✗ crept up him on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a stealthy approach, literal or figurative, and the progressive is normal: the deadline is creeping up on us again.
entries.passive: restricted. Natural with a personal subject and no agent, especially in the -ing form: nobody likes being crept up on in a parking garage. It gets clumsy with a by-phrase — ✗ the bird was crept up on by the cat — and the time sense refuses it: ✗ we have been crept up on by the deadline.
entries.see also: creep up, come upon, catch up with

entries.meaning: To take a shortcut through something, or to run through groups that normally divide.
examples: We cut across the field instead of following the road.
She cuts across the parking lot every morning.
The measure cut across party lines.
Complaints cut across every department we surveyed.
Grief cuts across everything else people disagree about.

senses.head: Take a shortcut through
examples: We cut across the field instead of following the road.
She cuts across the parking lot every morning.

senses.head: Run through and beyond ordinary divisions
body: Of issues, tastes, and opinions. (выходить за рамки, объединять)
examples: The measure cut across party lines.
Complaints cut across every department we surveyed.
Grief cuts across everything else people disagree about.

entries.русский: срезать путь через; выходить за рамки, пересекать (границы групп)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows across: cut across the lawn, never ✗ cut the lawn across.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: Both. Sense 1 is action — dynamic: we cut across the field instead of following the road. Sense 2 (run through ordinary divisions) is stative, a standing property rather than an event, and sits badly in the progressive: ✗ grief is cutting across everything else.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the field was cut across means something else entirely (a cut made in it), and the figurative sense refuses promotion: ✗ party lines were cut across by the measure, ✗ every department was cut across by the complaints.
entries.see also: cut through, come across

entries.meaning: To remove something by cutting; in editing, to switch briefly to another shot.
examples: Cut away the dead growth before you feed the plant.
The surgeon cut the scar tissue away first.
Once you cut it away you can see how far the rot went.
The director cuts away to the crowd every time the coach yells.
They cut away just before the punch lands.

senses.head: Remove by cutting
examples: Cut away the dead growth before you feed the plant.
