The surgeon cut the scar tissue away first.
Once you cut it away you can see how far the rot went.

senses.head: Switch to another shot
body: No object; the new shot follows to. (перейти к другому кадру)
examples: The director cuts away to the crowd every time the coach yells.
They cut away just before the punch lands.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on way; the noun cutaway moves it to cut
entries.русский: срезать, обрезать (лишнее); перейти к другому кадру
entries.separable: yes — cut away the rotten wood, cut the rotten wood away, cut it away, never ✗ cut away it. In the film sense there is no object: cut away to the crowd.
entries.register: everyday — the second sense is film and television jargon
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, removing material (cut away the dead growth) and switching shots (the director cuts away to the crowd); progressive fine in both: they're cutting away to a commercial.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1, and it is the usual form in surgical and repair writing: the scar tissue was cut away first, once the rot has been cut away you can see the damage. No passive of the film sense, which has no object: ✗ the crowd was cut away to.
entries.see also: cut off, cut out, cast off

entries.meaning: To reduce something, or to prune a plant hard.
examples: We had to cut back after the second kid.
The plant cut back to four days a week.
Cut back the hydrangeas in March.
He cut the raspberries back almost to the ground.
If they get leggy, cut them back and they'll come again.

senses.head: Reduce spending, hours, or production
examples: We had to cut back after the second kid.
The plant cut back to four days a week.

senses.head: Prune hard
examples: Cut back the hydrangeas in March.
He cut the raspberries back almost to the ground.
If they get leggy, cut them back and they'll come again.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on back; the noun cutback moves it to cut
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — cut back the roses, cut the roses back, cut them back, never ✗ cut back them. In the "spend less" sense there is no object at all, and what you reduce follows on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, reducing (we had to cut back after the second kid) and pruning (cut back the hydrangeas in March); progressive fine: the plant is cutting back to four days a week.
entries.passive: yes in the pruning sense: the raspberries were cut back almost to the ground. No passive of the reduce sense, which takes no object — ✗ the plant was cut back to four days would be read as pruning; say production was cut or hours were reduced.
entries.see also: cut back on, cut down, cost out

entries.meaning: To use, spend, or consume less of something without giving it up entirely.
examples: The doctor told him to cut back on salt.
We cut back on travel and kept everyone employed.
She has cut back on shifts since the baby.
If you cut back on it slowly, the headaches are milder.
The city cut back on overtime rather than lay anyone off.
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: cut back on sugar, cut back on it. ✗ cut sugar back on, ✗ cut back sugar on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate reduction, and the progressive is normal: she's been cutting back on shifts since the baby.
entries.passive: restricted — possible but stiff, and only without an agent: overtime was cut back on rather than cut altogether. Avoid it with by: ✗ salt was cut back on by him. Plain was reduced is the natural passive.
entries.see also: cut back, cut down on

entries.meaning: To fell something, to reduce something, or (in older writing) to kill.
examples: They cut down the elm that had been there since 1940.
He cut the dead one down in an afternoon.
Cut the introduction down to a page.
I've cut down to one cup a day.
If it runs long, cut it down.
A whole generation was cut down in four years.
The fever cut him down at thirty-one.

senses.head: Fell, chop down
examples: They cut down the elm that had been there since 1940.
He cut the dead one down in an afternoon.

senses.head: Reduce, shorten
body: Of text, costs, and habits. (сократить, урезать)
examples: Cut the introduction down to a page.
I've cut down to one cup a day.
If it runs long, cut it down.

senses.head: Kill, strike down
body: Formal and literary; usually passive. (сразить, скосить)
examples: A whole generation was cut down in four years.
The fever cut him down at thirty-one.

entries.separable: yes — cut down the tree, cut the tree down, cut it down, never ✗ cut down it. In the "consume less" sense there is no object and the thing follows on.
entries.register: everyday — the "kill" sense is formal and literary
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: felling (they cut down the elm), reducing (cut the introduction down to a page), and the literary killing sense (the fever cut him down at thirty-one). Progressive fine: I'm cutting down to one cup a day.
entries.passive: yes, and in sense 3 the passive is the usual form: a whole generation was cut down in four years. Also the elm was cut down last spring, the introduction has been cut down to a page. No passive of the intransitive I've cut down to one cup a day.
entries.see also: cut down on, cut back, cut out

entries.meaning: To do or consume less of something. Interchangeable with cut back on in almost every context.
examples: I'm trying to cut down on screen time.
She cut down on red meat without giving it up.
Better routing cut down on fuel costs by a third.
He never quit, but he cut down on it a lot.
Anything that cuts down on paperwork is worth trying.
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: cut down on coffee, cut down on it. ✗ cut coffee down on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual reduction of consumption or activity, comfortable in the progressive: I'm trying to cut down on screen time.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but awkward, and only agentless: screen time has been cut down on all year. ✗ red meat was cut down on by her is bad; native writers use was reduced or she cut down on it.
entries.see also: cut back on, cut down

entries.meaning: To interrupt, to pull in front of someone, to switch on by itself, or to give someone a share.
examples: She cut in before he could finish the sentence.
Sorry to cut in, but the car's being towed.
A pickup cut in about a foot from our bumper.
They cut the two engineers in for a point each.
They cut him in for ten percent.
Cut me in on the next one and I'll front the deposit.
The backup generator cuts in within about four seconds.
The compressor cut in and the lights dimmed.

senses.head: Interrupt a conversation
examples: She cut in before he could finish the sentence.
Sorry to cut in, but the car's being towed.

senses.head: Pull in front of another driver
examples: A pickup cut in about a foot from our bumper.

senses.head: Give someone a share
body: Separable, and the deal follows on. (включить в долю)
examples: They cut the two engineers in for a point each.
They cut him in for ten percent.
Cut me in on the next one and I'll front the deposit.

senses.head: (Of a motor or pump) start automatically
examples: The backup generator cuts in within about four seconds.
The compressor cut in and the lights dimmed.

entries.русский: перебить, вмешаться в разговор; подрезать (на дороге); включить в долю
entries.separable: yes, but only in the "share the profits" sense — cut me in on the deal, cut him in, never ✗ cut in him. In the other senses there is no object at all.
entries.register: everyday — the "share the profits" sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: interrupting (she cut in before he could finish), pulling in front (a pickup cut in), giving a share (they cut him in for ten percent), and a motor starting by itself (the compressor cut in).
entries.passive: restricted — yes only in the share sense, where it is idiomatic: he was cut in for ten percent, the two engineers were cut in for a point each. No passive of the other three, which take no object: ✗ the conversation was cut in, ✗ the generator is cut in within four seconds.
entries.see also: cut into, cut off, come between

entries.meaning: To eat away at something, to slice into it, or to break into a conversation.
examples: The new fees cut into our margin badly.
Practice cuts into every weekday evening.
The rope cut into his palms.
She cut into the cake before anyone had sung.
He cut into the argument with a question nobody could answer.

senses.head: Reduce, eat away at
body: Of profits, time, and margins. (урезать, съедать)
examples: The new fees cut into our margin badly.
Practice cuts into every weekday evening.

senses.head: Slice into something physically
examples: The rope cut into his palms.
She cut into the cake before anyone had sung.

senses.head: Break into a conversation
examples: He cut into the argument with a question nobody could answer.

entries.русский: урезать, съедать (время, прибыль); врезаться в; вклиниться (в разговор)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows into: cut into our profits, never ✗ cut our profits into.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: eroding (the new fees cut into our margin), slicing (the rope cut into his palms), and interrupting (he cut into the argument with a question); progressive fine: practice is cutting into every weekday evening.
entries.passive: no in practice. The prepositional passive is marginal at best — ✗ our margin was cut into by the new fees, ✗ his palms were cut into by the rope — and the interrupt sense refuses it outright: ✗ the argument was cut into. Say the fees ate into our margin or our margin shrank.
entries.see also: cut in, cut through, cut back on

entries.meaning: To free something by cutting, to sever ties with someone, or to let yourself go.
examples: He cut the trailer loose and drove on.
The label cut her loose after one album.
If the deal is that bad, cut it loose.
Once the last table cleared, the kitchen staff cut loose.
He hardly drinks, but at a wedding he cuts loose.

senses.head: Free by cutting; sever ties
examples: He cut the trailer loose and drove on.
The label cut her loose after one album.
If the deal is that bad, cut it loose.

senses.head: Let yourself go, have a wild time
examples: Once the last table cleared, the kitchen staff cut loose.
He hardly drinks, but at a wedding he cuts loose.

entries.русский: отвязать, обрубить связь; оторваться, дать себе волю
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — cut the boat loose, cut loose the boat, cut it loose, never ✗ cut loose it. In the "let go and enjoy yourself" sense there is no object.
entries.register: everyday — the "enjoy yourself" sense is informal, and thoroughly American
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, freeing or severing (he cut the trailer loose) and letting yourself go (at a wedding he cuts loose). Loose here is a resultative adjective describing the object, not an ordinary particle — compare cut it free.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense, and it is common of people: she was cut loose after one album, the trailer had been cut loose miles back. No passive of the enjoy-yourself sense, which has no object: ✗ the kitchen staff was cut loose would mean they were fired.
entries.see also: cut off, cast off, cut up

entries.meaning: To sever, disconnect, isolate, interrupt, or disinherit — one verb doing all six jobs.
examples: Cut off the stems at an angle before you put them in water.
He cut two inches off and it still didn't fit.
The power company cut off the electricity on a Friday.
They cut it off over a ninety-dollar balance.
The storm cut the valley off for six days.
She cut him off mid-sentence.
A van cut me off on the ramp.
His father cut him off the year he dropped out.

senses.head: Sever, remove by cutting
examples: Cut off the stems at an angle before you put them in water.
He cut two inches off and it still didn't fit.

senses.head: Disconnect a service
examples: The power company cut off the electricity on a Friday.
They cut it off over a ninety-dollar balance.

senses.head: Isolate, block access
examples: The storm cut the valley off for six days.

senses.head: Interrupt someone
examples: She cut him off mid-sentence.

senses.head: Pull dangerously in front of a driver
examples: A van cut me off on the ramp.

senses.head: Disinherit or stop supporting
body: Often cut off without a cent. (лишить наследства, перестать содержать)
examples: His father cut him off the year he dropped out.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on off; the noun and adjective cutoff move it to cut
entries.русский: отрезать; отключить (свет, воду); отрезать от мира; перебить; подрезать; лишить наследства
entries.separable: yes — cut off the power, cut the power off, and with a pronoun it must split: cut it off, never ✗ cut off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: severing (cut off the stems at an angle), disconnecting a service, isolating, interrupting (she cut him off mid-sentence), pulling in front of a driver, and disinheriting (his father cut him off).
entries.passive: yes, in every sense, and in sense 3 the passive is the normal form: the valley was cut off for six days, the electricity was cut off on a Friday, he was cut off without a cent, I got cut off on the ramp.
entries.see also: cut out, cut in, cut loose, cut away

entries.meaning: To remove by cutting, to stop doing something, to quit working, or — in the passive — to be suited to something.
examples: She cut out the pattern and pinned it to the fabric.
He cut the article out and mailed it to me.
Cut it out — she's trying to sleep.
I cut out soda in January and lost eight pounds.
The outboard cut out half a mile from shore.
The distributor cut them out of the deal entirely.
He wasn't cut out for sales.
I'm not sure she's cut out for the night shift.

senses.head: Remove by cutting
examples: She cut out the pattern and pinned it to the fabric.
He cut the article out and mailed it to me.

senses.head: Stop doing something
examples: Cut it out — she's trying to sleep.
I cut out soda in January and lost eight pounds.

senses.head: (Of an engine or a motor) stop suddenly
examples: The outboard cut out half a mile from shore.

senses.head: Exclude someone
examples: The distributor cut them out of the deal entirely.

senses.head: Be cut out for — be suited to
body: Passive only, and always negative or questioning in practice. (быть созданным для)
examples: He wasn't cut out for sales.
I'm not sure she's cut out for the night shift.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on out; the noun cutout moves it to cut
entries.русский: вырезать; прекратить; заглохнуть (о двигателе); исключить (из рациона); быть созданным для (be cut out for)
entries.separable: yes — cut out the coupon, cut the coupon out, and with a pronoun it must split: cut it out, never ✗ cut out it. That is why the idiom is cut it out and never ✗ cut out it.
entries.transitive: either — no object in the "stop working" sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: removing by cutting (she cut out the pattern), stopping (cut it out), an engine quitting (the outboard cut out), excluding (they cut them out of the deal). Sense 5, be cut out for, is a fixed stative adjectival passive — a standing fitness, not an event: he wasn't cut out for sales.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1–2 and 4: the article was cut out and mailed to me, soda has been cut out entirely, they were cut out of the deal. Sense 5 exists only in the passive, with no active counterpart: ✗ sales didn't cut him out for. No passive of the engine sense: ✗ the outboard was cut out.
entries.see also: cut off, cut down, cut away

entries.meaning: To take a shortcut through a place, or to get past something that is slowing everyone down.
examples: We cut through the alley to save five minutes.
Her one question cut through an hour of hedging.
Somebody has to cut through the red tape or the permit will sit there.
A siren cut through the noise of the crowd.
Good writing cuts through; clever writing rarely does.
entries.русский: пройти напрямик через; пробиться сквозь (бюрократию, шум)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows through: cut through the alley, never ✗ cut the alley through.
entries.transitive: yes — the object comes after the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, taking a shortcut (we cut through the alley) and getting past an obstruction (her one question cut through an hour of hedging); progressive fine: the siren was cutting through the noise.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the alley was cut through is read as a hole being made in it, not a shortcut, and the figurative sense is barely better: ✗ the red tape was cut through by somebody. Use an active subject, or switch to get past / break through.
entries.see also: cut across, cut into, come through

entries.meaning: To divide something into pieces, to fool around, or (in British use) to be badly upset.
examples: Cut up the onions while the pan heats.
He cut the cardboard up small enough for the bin.
Wash the potatoes and cut them up.
The two of them cut up in the back of the class all year.
He cuts up the second a camera appears.
She was terribly cut up about the dog.
He was still cut up about it a year later.

senses.head: Divide into pieces
examples: Cut up the onions while the pan heats.
He cut the cardboard up small enough for the bin.
Wash the potatoes and cut them up.

senses.head: Clown around, misbehave
body: American and informal; no object. (дурачиться, паясничать)
examples: The two of them cut up in the back of the class all year.
He cuts up the second a camera appears.

senses.head: Be cut up — be badly upset
body: British; Americans say torn up or broken up. (быть расстроенным, убитым)
examples: She was terribly cut up about the dog.
He was still cut up about it a year later.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on up; the noun cutup, meaning a clown, moves it to cut
entries.русский: нарезать, разрезать на куски; дурачиться, паясничать
entries.separable: yes — cut up the onions, cut the onions up, cut them up, never ✗ cut up them. The "clown around" sense takes no object.
entries.register: everyday — the "clown around" sense is informal and American; the "upset" sense is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the first two senses, dividing (cut up the onions) and clowning around (he cuts up the second a camera appears). Sense 3, the British be cut up, is a stative adjectival passive describing a state of distress: she was terribly cut up about the dog.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1: the potatoes were washed and cut up, the cardboard had been cut up small enough for the bin. No passive of the clown-around sense, which has no object: ✗ the class was cut up in. Sense 3 is passive in form only — it has no active: ✗ the dog cut her up.
entries.see also: cut down, cut off, cut loose
